1.pericope_label: It was determined that we should sail into Italy: the guard, the ship, and the companions

schools.summary: Gill sees three determinations concurring — the decree of God made known to Paul, his own resolution upon it, which was why he appealed, and the sentence of Festus, which settled the time as well. He reports that the Latin, Syriac and Arabic read “he” and the Ethiopic reads “Paul” outright, while the Greek copies read “we”. On the port he argues for an African Adrumetum built by Tyrians, whose Phoenician name he renders the court of death, from bad air or a dangerous haven. Calvin thinks Luke records the sea journey chiefly to show that Paul was brought to Rome by the hand of God, whose glory appeared even on the way, so that the journey itself confirmed his apostleship; and he marks that though Paul is handed over with other prisoners, the Lord will soon put a great difference between him and the evil-doers bound beside him. Of the band he can only guess at the old praetorian cohort. Of Aristarchus he notices that many went up to Jerusalem and two remain; he will not blame the absent, who may have been hindered or dismissed, but praises this man as rich enough to bear three years of charges away from home, and crossing the sea after an imprisonment to serve at Rome under many reproaches.

Henry puts the two determinations sharply: it was determined by the counsel of God before the counsel of Festus, for whatever men intended God had work for him at Rome. In the company of prisoners he hears an old note, Paul linked with malefactors as Christ was with the thieves, since it is no new thing for the innocent to be numbered with transgressors; and he observes that later in the chapter these men nearly cost him his life, while for his sake they kept theirs.

Clarke reports the name of the Augustan cohort as found on an ancient marble, and on the port reports Gill's African guess and rejects it for the Mysian town opposite Mitylene. Wesley says only that Aristarchus and Luke went by choice, not ashamed of Paul's bonds.

Barnes finds the Greek manuscripts uniform in reading “we” and takes the word as proof that Luke was of the party, though whether at his own charge or the government's is not said; he takes the Augustan band for a division named in the emperor's honour. Ellicott sets out three accounts of that band: that it was levied at Sebaste, where Sebastene cavalry is known; that it answers to the equestrian young men whom Nero had lately formed into a claque and named Augustani, which he thinks likeliest; or that its officer is the Julius Priscus later made a prefect of the praetorian cohorts. He holds that the word for “other” prisoners implies a different class, and supposes they too had appealed, since otherwise there was no object in sending them to Rome; he adds that there was little direct traffic between Caesarea and Rome, so the passage had to be made in one vessel after another, and dates the embarkation to late August, reckoning back from the Fast; and he infers that Aristarchus had waited out the two years in Palestine and meant only to return to Thessalonica. Robertson calls the construction awkward Greek, an infinitive of the kind the Greek Old Testament uses for a Hebrew form, and judges that the detail and accuracy of this narrative throw more light on ancient seafaring than all other sources together — yet its author, exact as he is with sea terms, writes like a landsman and not a sailor. He confesses we do not know why the cohort is called Augustan, suggesting the imperial grain service; thinks the other prisoners condemned men bound for the shows; calls the vessel a coaster going home for the winter; and notes Ramsay's suggestion that Luke and Aristarchus travelled as slaves, friends not being permitted, though he thinks Luke got leave as physician.

sides.position: a cohort levied at Sebaste, or Nero’s newly formed Augustani, or the cohort of the Julius Priscus known from Tacitus — the second likeliest
a division of the legion named in the emperor’s honour, its name attested on an ancient marble
the old praetorian band
we do not really know; possibly part of the imperial grain service, since Julius takes charge in the corn ship

debates.question: Where was the Adramyttium of the ship’s name?

sides.position: an African Adrumetum built by Tyrians, its Phoenician name meaning the court of death
the Mysian town opposite Mitylene

themes: it was determined that we should sail into Italy
a centurion of Augustus’ band, named Julius
a ship of Adramyttium
Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, being with us

3.pericope_label: From Sidon under Cyprus to Myra, and thence with difficulty to the Fair Havens

schools.summary: Gill holds with Ellicott that the congregation of Sidon's Christians were Paul's friends there, and reports that the top sail was the mark of an Alexandrian ship, no others being allowed to spread one or obliged to strike it in port; he also takes the ship's slow sailing from the Syriac, which refers it to her heavy lading. Calvin turns the centurion's courtesy into a duty: Paul could have hidden in so large a city, but was bound by the oracle and could not withdraw from his calling; and since the centurion, who might have left him in the stench of the ship, had let him go to friends, he could not have saved his own life at that man's peril without treachery — nor may we let anyone suffer for having treated us kindly.

Clarke traces the kind treatment to the impression Paul had made on Agrippa and Festus, and guesses that the soldier chained to his arm fared well on his account; he reports the many spellings of Myra and Grotius's conjecture that all are corrupt for Limyra, adds the ship's heavy lading to the contrary wind, and finds no city of Lasea remaining, preferring to read Alassa and guessing at a place near Gortyna. Wesley thinks Julius may have heard Paul's defence, and sums up the last verse: the Fair Havens keep their name, but Lasea is utterly lost, with many more of the hundred cities for which Crete was renowned.

Ellicott and Robertson both point out that the adverb for the centurion's courtesy is literally “philanthropically”, the one adding this to the other instances where officials thought well of Paul, the other that Julius was kind to him throughout. On the leave granted they differ in emphasis: Ellicott renders the phrase as availing himself of their care and thinks it a provision of clothing and comforts, welcome after two years in custody, while Robertson allows it may have been hospitality but wonders whether medical attention was needed after so long a confinement. Barnes recalls that Felix had allowed the same, and supposes a man who passed that way so often had friends in every principal city; Robertson notes that this is Paul's first visit, though there were Christians in Phoenicia already. Barnes explains that to sail under Cyprus is to hug its coast, keeping the island between the ship and the westerlies; Ellicott makes the wind north-west and has them take the channel between Cyprus and Cilicia, sheltered as far as the promontory now called Capo Andrea; Robertson names these winds Etesian. Ellicott calls Myra a former metropolis with a theatre and aqueduct still standing, adds that Alexandrian traders avoided the African coast for fear of the Syrtis, and reckons that in many days they had not made the hundred and twenty miles from Myra to Cnidus, the Etesian gales blowing through August, so that with the coast trending north the only course was south for the lee of Crete, reached at Cape Salmone. Robertson makes it a hundred and thirty miles and marks Cnidus as the point where the land's protection ceased, the verb for sailing slowly occurring nowhere else in scripture; he adds that no disciples are named here, nor at Lasea, Melita or Syracuse. On the anchorage Barnes doubts it was a harbour at all and calls it an open road which an old geographer named the fair shore, while Ellicott and Robertson fix it two miles east of Cape Matala, the latter adding that it is no place to winter.

debates.question: Where was the port called the Fair Havens, and what was it?

sides.position: not properly a harbour but an open road, good anchorage for a time, called by an old geographer the fair shore
a sheltered anchorage two miles east of Cape Matala, and no place to winter

themes: Julius courteously entreated Paul, and gave him liberty to go unto his friends
we sailed under Cyprus, because the winds were contrary
a ship of Alexandria sailing into Italy
the fair havens, nigh whereunto was the city of Lasea

9.pericope_label: Paul admonishes them, and the centurion believes the master and the owner of the ship

schools.summary: Gill has it plainly from a spirit of prophecy, by which Paul foresaw and foretold; he wonders whether one man or two is meant by the master and the owner, and describes the governor as sitting aloft in the stern at the helm, giving orders others executed, his skill lying in the stars, the winds, and the sands. Calvin argues the identification of the Fast at length, rejecting the four fasts appointed after the captivity and refusing to refer the word to hunger, wheat being still in the ship. He will not have the centurion reproved: what else should he have done, deferring to Paul in other things but knowing him unskilled in sailing, and almost compelled by a haven not fit to winter in? To yield to the expert is the part of a modest man, and the pilot proposed no venture into the open sea but a run to the next port, almost in view. Luke sets it down, he says, that we may know Paul was furnished from the first with the sense of the Spirit and saw further than the masters, whether by oracle or secret inspiration we cannot tell.

Clarke identifies the Fast as the day of atonement and notes that to sail after this feast was proverbially dangerous among the ancient Jews, and allows that Paul's warning might have come either from the Spirit or from his own knowledge of the season. Wesley dates the Fast to the twenty-fifth of September and calls it an ill time of sailing, not only because winter was approaching but because of the sudden storms still common in the Mediterranean then; on the centurion he states the rule and the exception together: believe a craftsman in his own craft, yet at the greatest need a real Christian will often advise better.

Barnes identifies the Fast with the day of atonement at the autumnal equinox and refuses to choose whether Paul's foresight was natural or inspired, since the knowledge might have come from the season and the look of an unfit ship, yet nothing forbids believing the Spirit guided him. Ellicott adds that the Jewish sailing season ran from Pentecost to Tabernacles, five days after the Fast, and infers from Luke's naming the one and not the other that the week between them is meant; he finds the tone of the warning that of a man speaking from observation rather than supernatural foresight, remembering the three shipwrecks behind Paul and an acquaintance with Crete close enough that he may have known the harbour; and he guesses that the date stuck in Luke's memory because Paul kept the day, however little he cared to impose it on others. Robertson has the ancients count the sea unsafe from October until mid-March, thinks they left Caesarea in August in ample time to have reached Rome had the winds served, and finds nothing strange in a Gentile writer dating by a Jewish fast, since Paul does the same. He thinks it remarkable that a prisoner should venture advice at all and keep venturing it, notes that the term for hurt is properly an insult which Josephus uses of the violence of the elements, and reports that the papyri always give the second seaman's title the sense of captain rather than owner, setting the centurion above both, answerable for soldiers, prisoners and cargo, and afraid of being blamed at Rome for timidity when the wheat was wanted. Ellicott thinks it natural that he should trust the experts rather than the enthusiastic Rabbi in his charge.

debates.question: Was Paul’s warning prophecy or seamanship?

sides.position: a spirit of prophecy, by which he foresaw and foretold
the tone of a man speaking from observation rather than supernatural foresight, three shipwrecks and a knowledge of Crete behind him
either, or both — the knowledge might have come from the season and the unfit ship, yet nothing forbids believing the Spirit guided him

themes: sailing was now dangerous, because the fast was now already past
I perceive that this voyage will be with hurt and much damage
the centurion believed the master and the owner of the ship
no lives were in fact lost, though all else was

12.pericope_label: The vote to leave the Fair Havens, and the harbour of Phenice

schools.summary: Gill suspects the name of the Fair Havens was given by antiphrasis, a summer road with nothing to break the sea in foul weather.

Henry weighs the motives for leaving: bleak lying in winter, provisions perhaps scarce and dear, and men running upon a mischief to avoid an inconvenience, as we often do. Some were for staying rather than venturing with the weather so uncertain — better safe in an incommodious harbour than lost in a tempestuous sea — but they were outvoted. He then turns from the place to the sailing: they set out with the south wind blowing softly and kept close along the coast without fear of rock or quicksand, but men who put to sea with the fairest gale do not know what they may meet, and must not reckon the point gained. Here, he says, they looked at second causes and read the smiling wind as a promise, crediting it above the word of God in Paul's mouth. What came was not merely contrary but violent, a wind God commanded out of his treasuries to bring glory to himself and reputation to his servant; and Henry marks the difference from the storm sent after Jonah, Paul going on in his duty and not running from it. The ship was tossed from wave to wave, and he borrows the psalm — mounting to heaven, going down to the depths, staggering like drunken men at their wits' end. She could not bear up into the wind, so they furled what would only have endangered them and let her drive where the sea carried her; and they had been near their quiet haven, he thinks, pleasing themselves with the thought of wintering there, when it was taken from them.

Clarke identifies the two winds as the libs, named from Libya, and the chorus or caurus, quoting Virgil's line on the north-westers ever blowing cold. Wesley describes the harbour more shortly as one with a double opening.

Barnes calls the Fair Havens anchorage for a squall, not a permanent harbour, and reads the vote the other way from the rest, thinking the majority agreed with Paul that the open sea should not be attempted before winter was over, the run to Phenice contradicting nothing; he takes the two wind-names for the harbour's own bearings and reconstructs a curved inlet entered from the south-west and turning to the north-west, proof against wind and sea alike. Ellicott says the anchorage sheltered them from the north-westers but lay open elsewhere, and denies Barnes's approach: the words are names of winds and not points of the compass, and the harbour is described as looking down them, in the direction they blow, so that it faced north-east and south-east. On that reading he identifies it with the modern Lutro, which Ptolemy names and which Greek pirates use still, and adds a votive tablet from the reign of Nerva, found near the spot and raised by an agent of the fleet with an Alexandrian pilot — the word is Luke's own — from which he infers that a corn ship had wintered at that very harbour and left the tablet in thanks for coming through. Robertson renders the phrase “unfit for wintering”, a compound occurring nowhere else, takes the decision for a formal vote of the ship's officers on the question Paul had raised, and sets the two constructions of the wind-names side by side, admitting that the choice turns on a preposition; he follows Ramsay to Lutro, on the ground that sailors describe a harbour as it looks to them going in.

debates.question: Which way did the harbour of Phenice face, and which modern site is it?

sides.position: the wind-names give the harbour’s own bearings — a curved inlet entered from the south-west and turning north-west
the words name winds, not compass points; the harbour looks down them, facing north-east and south-east, which identifies it with the modern Lutro

debates.question: What did the majority actually vote for?

sides.position: to press on and face the immediate risk for the sake of a better winter harbour
they agreed with Paul that the open sea should not be attempted before winter was over; the short run to Phenice contradicted nothing

themes: the haven was not commodious to winter in
the more part advised to depart thence also
Phenice, an haven of Crete
when the south wind blew softly, supposing that they had obtained their purpose

13.pericope_label: Euroclydon: the ship caught, and the work done under Clauda

schools.summary: Gill has the ship snatched up bodily, and takes the slow sailing from the Syriac, which lays it to her heavy lading. Calvin reads the whole episode morally. The mariners, having got some way with the weather fair, had derided the warning, as men grow proud when fortune favours them, and were now punished for it; they spared neither cargo nor tackle, and when all was tried they despaired, the dark sky serving them for a grave. God meant by it to make the coming rescue more notable, and left his servant to labour with the rest until he seemed past recovery; and though Luke records no prayer, it is likely that while others cursed heaven and earth he was quietly waiting the Lord's leisure.

Clarke follows Shaw, who reconstructed the course from the drift itself and concluded that the wind set first east by north and afterwards nearly east by south, Euroclydon being then what a Levanter is now, a name for any tempest from that arc; Shaw thought the rival reading insupportable. Clarke also adds the heavy lading to the contrary wind. Wesley calls the wind a hurricane carrying them no one way but tossing them backward and forward.

Barnes explains that a headwind from the west had veered south, and though not wholly fair seemed enough to coast by; he takes the wind for a hurricane veering about rather than a steady wind from one point, of the sort now called a Levanter, and derives the name from words for wind and wave. Ellicott has the pilot and owner conclude that all was smooth sailing and stand across the bay for Phenice, hugging the shore for fear of open water, and devotes a note to the adverb for “close in shore”, which the Vulgate and others mistook for a place-name, so that the versions have them leaving Assos, making for it, or sighting it — though the Assos men know lies far north and no Cretan town of the name exists. He reports Euro-aquilo from some of the best copies, a hybrid unknown to Greek and Latin writers but fitting the phenomena as east by north, and holds that Euroclydon, if genuine, must be a word Luke heard the sailors use; and he raises a grammatical difficulty, that the pronoun is feminine where the word for ship is neuter, so that it must refer to Crete, of whose three possible senses only “rushed down from it” agrees with a gale that carried them southward. Robertson says the verb for blowing softly occurs nowhere else, notes that they were so confident they did not even take up the boat towing astern, reports Page's view that Euroclydon is a corruption of the other form, reaches Ellicott's result from the case of the pronoun, the Cretan mountains rising above seven thousand feet, and quotes the judgment that the squall left no time to furl the great mainsail. He and Ellicott both dwell on the phrase for bearing up, literally to look the wind in the eye, a figure the more vivid because Greek vessels carried a painted eye on the prow; and Robertson takes the helps for cables passed under the hull and set up tight on deck, a frapping the more needed in ancient ships because of their heavy mast, reckoning after Smith that thirteen days of such a drift would run very nearly the distance to Malta. Ellicott sets the order of work under the island: first to get aboard the boat that had been towing, hard both because the vessel would not lie head to wind and because it was probably swamped; Barnes insists the point was not a landing but the boat's rescue.

debates.question: What was the wind’s name, and from what quarter did it blow?

sides.position: Euroclydon, from words for wind and wave; a Levanter veering about rather than a steady wind, setting first east by north and then east by south
Euro-aquilo, from the best copies — a hybrid word meaning east by north; Euroclydon, if genuine, is what Luke heard the sailors say

debates.question: What does the feminine pronoun in “arose against it” refer to?

sides.position: to Crete — and of the three possible senses only “rushed down from it” fits a gale that carried them south

themes: there arose against it a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon
the ship was caught, and could not bear up into the wind
running under a certain island which is called Clauda
undergirding the ship, fearing lest they should fall into the quicksands

17.pericope_label: Undergirding, lightening, and the loss of all hope

schools.summary: Gill describes what the ancients read in the sky before the loadstone was known — the sun's rays and colour, the moon's size and hue, and above all the two Bears, the Greeks steering by the greater and the Phoenicians by the lesser.

Clarke describes the practice, still called frapping, of passing a rope under the bow and along the keel and setting both ends up on deck, and cites with Barnes a Spanish man-of-war that took six turns of cable round herself to keep from opening. He will not hear of striking or slackening sail, since in such a sea they could have carried none; he passes over the yards and the anchor as useless and supposes the mast itself was cut away. He doubts the whole apprehension about the quicksands: from the direction of the drift the ship was never near the African coast, and the fear must be taken generally — men afraid of some shoal because they did not know where they were; it is wrong, he holds, to chart the course as though she had been carried down to the syrts at all, and he takes the Adria of the later verse for the sea about Sicily on an old scholiast's authority. He guesses the goods thrown over were cumbrous wares spoiling her trim. Wesley says only that the heavy goods went over, and that unnecessary masts were cut away.

Barnes joins the others in describing the frapping, adds that the quicksands shifted with the sea and could not be laid down on any chart, and takes the lowering of the gear for the cutting away of the mast, as is done in storms still; he takes the ship's furniture for spare anchors, cables and baggage, though he notes that anchors remained. Ellicott reaches back to the Corcyreans in Thucydides and to a line of Horace on keels that scarcely hold against the sea even when girdled with ropes; he holds the opposite of Barnes and Clarke on the gear, since had they struck sail she would have drifted the way they dreaded, and some canvas was needed to keep her steady, so what came down was the spars and rigging and above all the heavy yard that made her top-heavy. He takes the Syrtes for the terror of every Mediterranean sailor, quoting Lucan on a place that nature left neither sea nor land, and says the voyagers knew the gale was setting them that way and dared not run full before it; he calls the word for lightening a technical one for throwing a cargo overboard and argues that the act proves the leak was gaining in spite of the undergirding; he says the Greek word for the ship's furniture is wider than the English and takes in beds and luggage and movables of every kind; he reports that the better manuscripts have “they cast out” rather than “we”, and observes that on the received text the passengers were pressed into the work, showing how urgent the peril was; and he thinks the loss of all hope implies more than the gale — a sprung leak they could not stop, with hunger and exhaustion on top of it. Robertson adds that loose grain would shift and make her list, danger enough by itself, prefers the third person and dwells on the phrase “with their own hands”, a word found nowhere else, and watches the despair settle like a fog, asking whether Paul had lost hope with the rest.

debates.question: What was lowered when they “strake sail”?

sides.position: the mast itself was cut away or let down; in such a sea they could have carried no canvas at all
not the sail — had they struck sail she would have drifted the way they dreaded; what came down was the gear, spars and rigging and the heavy yard

debates.question: Were the Syrtes a real danger on this course?

sides.position: yes — the voyagers knew the gale was setting them that way and dared not run full before it
no — the drift never brought the ship near the African coast; the fear was general, of some unknown shoal

themes: they used helps, undergirding the ship
fearing lest they should fall into the quicksands, they strake sail
the next day they lightened the ship
neither sun nor stars in many days appeared

21.pericope_label: Paul stands forth: the long abstinence, and the reproof that opens the promise

schools.summary: Gill denies that food was wanting or any religious fast meant, laying the abstinence to a nausea bred of the tossing and the fear of death, and chiefly to want of time, every hand being employed on the ship. Calvin explains the timing of the speech: a moderate voice could never have been heard through the first uproar, and only when they were weary of working and howling, and sat still in a stupor, could a man be listened to, so Paul deferred his word until then. He admits the reproof looks unseasonable, Paul objecting their folly in a matter where they knew, and he knew, that he had no skill; but considering how hard men are to bring to soundness of mind, he judges the rebuke profitable, for his authority would have carried no weight unless they first understood that things had gone ill because they despised him. Chiding by itself is cruel, but tempered with a remedy it becomes part of the medicine. It took no small boldness, he adds, to say they ought to have obeyed, since by that word Paul testified he had ordered nothing rashly but what God prescribed; and though no revelation is recorded then, he knew the Spirit governed him, without which a drowning man's promise of safety would have been ridiculous.

Henry thinks they had resolved not to eat until they knew whether they were to live or die. He observes that through the distress Paul had hidden himself in the crowd and helped throw out the tackling, and that now, a prisoner still, he takes on himself the office of counsellor and comforter; and he presses the comparison with Jonah the other way, since among these seamen Paul was not, like Jonah among his, the cause of the storm but the comfort in it. He finds mercy in the reproof: they would not hear the warning, yet on acknowledging their folly they are met with comfort, God being compassionate to men in misery even when they have brought it on themselves; and most people undo themselves because they do not know when they are well off.

Clarke reports Wakefield's rendering, that there was a scarcity of provisions, and refuses it: the vessel was a corn ship whose wheat went over only later, so they had food and no appetite, and could hardly have dressed it. He grants that it is odd English to speak of gaining a loss but holds the version exact, distinguishing the harm done the vessel from the lost cargo.

Barnes lays the abstinence to the weather, the labour and the apprehension together, and agrees with Clarke that the Greek covers acquisition of good or evil alike. Ellicott adds that with no notion how long to a harbour, two hundred and seventy-six men had been put on short rations, and reads the silence behind Paul's standing forth: while the others broke into wailing, calling every man on his god as the sailors did in Jonah, the apostle had spent those hours communing with God, and comes forward because he knows his prayers are heard. On the last phrase he would render it “to have been spared”, arguing from parallels that to gain a harm is to escape it, and notes that the Geneva glossed it so while Tyndale and Cranmer took it as English readers still do. Robertson agrees on the abstinence, grain in plenty but seasickness and no fires, the medical writers using this word for loss of appetite; he calls the participle for standing forth a pictorial word which sets the solemnity of the scene before us, and reports the same dispute over the last phrase, the Revised Version carrying the negative over to the verb while Page and Thayer insist a man is said in Greek to gain a loss when, being in danger of it, he keeps clear.

debates.question: What does “to have gained this harm and loss” mean?

sides.position: the rendering is exact, odd as it sounds; the Greek covers acquisition of good or evil alike
render it “to have been spared” — to gain a harm is to escape it, making a profit of it by avoiding it
holders: Page and Thayer, as reported by Robertson

sides.position: it looks unseasonable, but was profitable, since his authority would have carried no weight until they saw that things had gone ill because they despised him
it is no small nature’s “I told you so” but an appeal to the earlier counsel in order to get the present one accepted

themes: after long abstinence Paul stood forth in the midst of them
ye should have hearkened unto me, and not have loosed from Crete
to have gained this harm and loss

22.pericope_label: The angel of the God whose I am: the promise of all their lives, and of a certain island

schools.summary: Gill supposes the vision came in a dream, or more likely while Paul was awake at prayer, and agrees with Ellicott that the detail about the island was given so that the event might prove no accident. Calvin turns to the risk of being thought rash: Paul promises so absolutely that all shall be saved that he must bring God forward as his witness, and Calvin is confident there was no fear of Satan's counterfeits here, since God never appeared to his servants without plain tokens and the discernment not to be deceived. He sees a further purpose in the naming: Paul extols his God among profane men, that they may learn not only that the true God is worshipped in Judea but that this prisoner worships him — and since they knew why he was in bonds, they might gather from an angel's coming down to him that his cause was approved above. There is in the words a secret commendation of the gospel, and a kind of triumph in his chains that he should be the minister of safety to so many and the interpreter of God. He asks how far the saints' integrity can profit the wicked, dismisses the notion that any man is a mediator earning salvation for others by merit, and answers that God has reasons for doing good to the reprobate on the faithful's account, as he blessed Potiphar's house for Joseph's sake. He thinks the doubt about which island deliberate, exercising the faith of his servant and proving to the rest that this came from the Spirit and not reason; and he notes drily that even so they did not believe him, since when land opened before them the sailors took it for a mainland and not an isle.

Clarke reads the design outward: to speak so confidently when every appearance was against him argued full persuasion, and the exactness with which the event answered the prediction must have shown these heathen that Paul's God was other than theirs; he counts the two hundred and seventy-six saved for one man's sake a proof of God's approbation, which must have shown the centurion his prisoner was innocent, and points out that the angel did not name the island. Wesley calls the phrase “whose I am, and whom I serve” a short compendium of religion holding faith, hope and love together, and presses the gift further — ask for souls and they shall be given, more than you hoped for — observing that the centurion, serving providence without knowing it, afterwards gave Paul the prisoners' lives, so that Paul was in God's sight master and pilot of the ship.

Barnes and Clarke remark how welcome such news would be to men from whom all hope had been taken, Barnes adding that his earlier counsel had proved wise, and insisting that the gift means preservation and not conversion. Ellicott dwells on the manner rather than the matter: look and tone must have helped, and in a scene of that misery it was something to see one man stand out with a quiet confidence that struck them before ever they heard the grounds of it. He contrasts Paul with others of an enthusiastic cast, in whom visions of the unseen world commonly breed terror, where in him they are a source of calm strength he can pass on to other men; he takes the charge not to fear as answering a prayer prompted not by fear of death but by dread that the purpose of a lifetime should fail on the verge of attainment, and notes that what follows shows the prayer reached beyond himself. He takes the phrase about service for one of worship rather than labour. Robertson observes that Paul had himself foretold loss of life as likely and now gives his reason for a changed view, and points out with Clarke that Paul was left in the dark as to which island it was.

debates.question: What was granted when God “gave” Paul all who sailed with him?

sides.position: preservation of their lives, not their conversion
their lives, and perhaps their souls also; ask for souls and they shall be given
God has many reasons for doing good to the reprobate on the faithful’s account, as he blessed Potiphar’s house for Joseph’s sake

themes: there shall be no loss of any man’s life among you
the angel of God, whose I am, and whom I serve
God hath given thee all them that sail with thee
we must be cast upon a certain island

27.pericope_label: The fourteenth night: soundings, four anchors, and the sailors’ attempt on the boat

schools.summary: Gill describes the ancient lead, filled with grease to bring up the bottom and tell rock from sand, has them dreading rocks as the depth fell from twenty to fifteen, and notices that Paul addressed the soldiers rather than the master and owner, likely in the plot. Calvin states the difficulty plainly: it is a marvel that Paul should say the rest could not be saved unless the sailors stayed, as if it lay in their power to void God's promise. His answer is that Paul is not separating God's power from his will and the means, since God does not commend his power so that men may sit still and despise them; had Hezekiah opened the gates to the enemy after the promise of deliverance, Isaiah would have cried that he was destroying himself and the city. God's hand is not tied to means, but when he appoints one he holds men's senses within the bounds he has set.
Henry adds that duty is ours and events God's, and that we do not trust God but tempt him when we claim his protection without using the means we have.

Clarke offers the smell of land, which seamen catch at a distance, as the ground of the sailors' surmise, explains the stern anchors by the shoaling water since even a ship's length mattered, and observes that the apostle, depending simply on God's promise, was the one watching over everybody's safety; he thinks the soldiers' cutting of the ropes a mark of accuracy, since they alone would have dared cross the crew. Wesley notices the pronoun: Paul says “ye cannot be saved”, not “we”.

Barnes says the ancients gave the name Adria not to the gulf only but to the whole sea between Greece, Italy and Africa, and that they wanted daylight to see their danger; he carries the argument over into salvation, since the certainty of an event is no reason against using means, the end being no more determined than the means, so that the decrees bred no neglect in Paul but the strongest exertion. Ellicott adds that Josephus, wrecked on the same run two years later, was picked up in the middle of Adria by a ship out of Cyrene; he and Robertson fix on the sound of breakers as what the sailors heard, name the Point of Koura, and note that a ship passing it today takes twenty fathoms and then fifteen. Ellicott says a complement of four anchors was ordinary, Caesar describing his ships as secured with four apiece; he and Robertson both note that the usual practice is to anchor by the bows, and both bring in the same witness, that Nelson anchored by the stern at Copenhagen and is said to have been reading this chapter on the morning of the battle. Robertson gives the seamanship — anchored from the prow she would have swung round and snapped her cables or presented her stern to the beach — and Ellicott the effect, that she now lay still and would be found at daybreak head to the shore, hearing the suspense of that night in Luke's few words. On the sailors' trick they agree: the boat was lowered on the pretence of carrying anchors out from the bow, which Ellicott notes would genuinely have required it, while the real design was to reach shore and leave the rest to their fate. Ellicott refuses to embarrass himself with the question of the promise, the promise being realised not by a blind fatalism but by man's co-operation; and Robertson observes that Paul had no notion of lying supinely down and leaving God to do it. Ellicott warns that sullen workers were a new danger.

debates.question: How can the promise stand if it depends on the sailors staying aboard?

sides.position: Paul is not separating God’s power from his will and the means; when God appoints a means he holds men within the bounds he has set
the certainty of an event is no reason against using means — the end is no more determined than the means, and the doctrine of decrees bred in Paul the strongest exertion
the question need not be pressed at all: the promise was to be realised not by a blind fatalism but by man’s co-operation

they cast four anchors out of the stern, and wished for the day

33.pericope_label: Paul persuades them to eat, gives thanks, and the ship is lightened again

schools.summary: Gill flatly denies that this was the Lord's supper, and takes it for the common bread of seafaring men, cataloguing ancient ships' provisions to show what such a meal was. Calvin admits it looks absurd that so great a multitude should fast a fortnight — one man might fast long, but it is scarce credible of a crowd — and answers that an unwonted abstinence is improperly called fasting, since they never filled their belly in all that time, men in sorrow almost loathing food. He values the thanksgiving as example: it was not merely Paul's daily custom but a testimony of confidence, and he called on God aloud that men drenched in sorrow might catch some hope — and so far succeeded that those who had forgotten through fear to care for their lives took food. He wants the number recorded for the miracle's sake: few but the sailors could swim, they were worn past moving their arms, and it is seldom that twenty swim in danger without one drowning another. In the second jettison he sees proof that Paul had at last prevailed, since it was still dark and no haven known — though, all unbelievers being unstable, the persuasion soon wore off.

Clarke asks what appetite men could have with death before them, and agrees it is by no means likely that the eucharist was celebrated: Paul would not celebrate such a mystery among ungodly sailors and soldiers, Jews and heathens together. Wesley turns the fast round: if a sense of present danger makes men forget to eat, we need not wonder when a sense of everlasting danger does the same, nor call that madness which may be the beginning of wisdom; and he puts the reason for eating bluntly, that they would swim ashore the better for it.

Barnes says the fourteen days cannot mean they had lived without food, only that danger and work left no room for a regular meal. Ellicott is most exact: the word is not the one used for entire abstinence, and it was physically impossible for two hundred and seventy-six men to go a fortnight without eating; scanty rations must have been doled out, but the suspense was such that nobody sat down to a meal. He argues that the noun rendered “health” means safety, the translators using the older, wider English sense, reads the proposal as more than practical insight — soldiers and sailors needed drawing together after the affair of the boat, and what they wanted was food for the body and company for the mind — and goes furthest on the bread: it was no more in itself than the natural incident of eating, but for the few Christians aboard it must have recalled the solemn breaking of bread, and would have been a feast of charity if not strictly eucharistic. He finds it a striking sight, all of them under the influence of one brave spirit, and suggests the wheat now thrown over was what had been kept back for provisions, the object being only to keep her afloat till they reached land. Barnes and Clarke identify the promise about the hair as proverbial, and Ellicott repeats that the assurance was not independent of their own co-operation. Robertson agrees that the word is safety and not spiritual salvation, takes the thanksgiving for the ordinary grace of a Hebrew household with Barnes, supposing that Paul and his friends had memories of the supper where the rest saw only a meal, and notes on the number that one great manuscript reads “about” rather than “two hundred”, though he blames a scribe, and that Josephus sailed to Italy with six hundred aboard.

debates.question: Was the breaking of bread a celebration of the Lord’s supper?

sides.position: certainly not — this was the common bread of seafaring men, and Paul would not celebrate such a mystery among ungodly sailors, Jews and heathens together
the ordinary grace of a Hebrew household, though Paul and his Christian companions would have had their own memories of the supper
in itself only the natural incident of a meal, yet for the few Christians aboard a reminder of the solemn breaking of bread, and at least a feast of charity

debates.question: Did they really go fourteen days without food?

sides.position: no — the word is not the usual one for entire abstinence, and it was physically impossible for so many; scanty rations were doled out but nobody sat down to a meal
an unwonted abstinence is improperly called fasting; they never filled their belly, men in sorrow almost loathing food

there shall not an hair fall from the head of any of you

39.pericope_label: They cast off the anchors and make for the beach, and run aground where two seas met

schools.summary: Gill takes the place where two seas met for an isthmus washed on both sides. Calvin takes the sharpest view of the grounding. It might seem at that moment that God had mocked his servant and Paul fed his fellow passengers on an empty hope; but God removed the error by prospering them, and it was fitting that their hearts should melt when the ship went to pieces, since despair increases the glory of a miracle. He governs his works so as to make some show of difficulty, until we learn that he will have the victory though all the world strive against him; and so he chose rather to draw them ashore from a wreck than bring the ship in whole.

Henry turns it to the reader: the vessel that rode out the storm in open water is dashed to pieces the moment she sticks fast, as a heart fixed in the world is lost while a heart kept above it, however tossed, has hope. They had the shore in sight and were wrecked in the harbour, which teaches us never to be secure; yet whatever the difficulty, a promised salvation shall without fail be brought to pass.

Clarke denies that the sail hoisted can be the mainsail, which would have been improper here, and makes it the jib run from the foremast to the bowsprit; he admits at the end that the nautical terms of this chapter are extremely difficult, and that he cannot be sure of having hit the sense everywhere. Wesley describes with the others the two paddle-rudders lashed up while the ship lay useless.

Barnes supposes they had been driven without one observation and were strangers to the island, renders the creek a bay and says the point of naming its shore is that the landing was level, not a face of rock; he notes that the Greek word for rudder is plural, and adds that the place where two seas met can hardly have been above water, being more likely a sandbank they never saw, while the breaking of the stern furnished the boards on which the company got ashore. Ellicott and Robertson give the better reason for their not knowing the land, that some of the sailors had likely been at Malta before but the bay lay well away from the great harbour where shipping went; Ellicott adds that the word for beach means a flat sandy one in Homer, and both note that the verb for thrusting the ship in is a sailor's term for running her aground. Ellicott, whose word for the sail survives in the Italian for a ship's largest, points out that in ancient rigging the largest was the foresail; Robertson agrees, and adds that the word for wind is a participle, the breeze that was blowing, which seems to imply the gale had slackened. Both agree on the topography: at the west end of the bay lies a small island the crew could not have known was one, and making for the beach they grounded on the bank between it and the coast, where two currents meet. The prow was fixed — Robertson's verb means fastened firmly, the adjective unshakeable — while the stern was being broken up, the tense in Ellicott and Robertson alike expressing an action still going on.

debates.question: What sail was hoisted to the wind?

sides.position: the mainsail, though Luther made it the mast and Grotius the foremast
not the mainsail, which would have been improper — the jib run from the foremast to the bowsprit
the foresail, which in ancient rigging was a ship’s largest sail

they committed themselves unto the sea, and loosed the rudder bands

42.pericope_label: The soldiers’ counsel, the centurion’s purpose, and all safe to land

schools.summary: Gill gives the deeper reason for the centurion's wish to save Paul, that a superior influence moved him, so that the word about Rome should stand. Calvin makes ingratitude the charge: they had Paul to thank twice over for their lives, and were now minded to kill the man for whose sake they should have spared the others; he had saved them like an angel of God and refreshed them on the day they were past hope, and they stick at nothing to destroy him. He sees a worse fault under the first — they had received the oracle that all their souls were given to Paul, and now, expecting to be saved with him dead, what are they doing but resisting God? The grace they tasted unwillingly in their extremity had lost its relish the moment the harbour came in sight. But he bids us mark the counsel of God, who both saved his servant and kept his promise by bringing to land the very men who did what they could to make it void — his goodness striving so with human wickedness.

Clarke has no patience with the soldiers: bloodthirsty and cowardly villains, whose trade was in human blood, who had watched these poor men bear the same distresses as themselves and now, when all who could swim might reach land, wanted them massacred lest they should. He thinks the centurion had seen the man was not only innocent but extraordinary, that the soldiers all got ashore by swimming, Roman training including how to swim, and that the prisoners were loosed; he will not let the escape pass as ordinary, since with the surf still violent the sick and the aged could hardly have come ashore on planks they had no skill to steer; and he closes the chapter with the reflection that the malice of the Jews and the fury of the elements were alike overruled, so that governors and nobles heard the gospel who otherwise would not, and Malta received it by way of a wreck, while assurance of God's will never excuses human means, Paul himself looking for a blessing on men's care. Wesley disposes of the counsel in three words: cruel, unjust, ungrateful; and hopes that some who came ashore received the apostle as a teacher sent from God, and found in that day's deliverance the earnest of a greater one.

Ellicott and Robertson point to Roman law, which put a guard's life in forfeit if his charge escaped, so that in killing the prisoners the soldiers saw their only chance of not being killed; Barnes offers the same reason but adds that they probably counted on its being taken for a drowning, and draws from it that men can be cruel in the very hour of God's mercy. Barnes traces the centurion's kindness from the start of the voyage, through the advice at Fair Havens and his prudence in the storm, and perhaps a belief that Paul stood under divine protection, drawing the lesson that benefit comes to sinners through the righteous, as ten would have saved Sodom; Robertson says the centurion knew by now how much they owed him. Ellicott observes that the landing was no rush of every man for himself: the centurion kept his head and could enforce discipline, sending the swimmers first to be on the beach ready to help the rest, and guesses that Paul, three times shipwrecked, was among them and may have suggested it. Robertson notes that the word for plank occurs nowhere else, the breaking up of the stern having furnished the timber, and he and Barnes take the outcome as the promise fulfilled, Robertson calling the narrative worthy of any historian in any age.

debates.question: Why did the soldiers propose to kill the prisoners?

sheer bloodthirsty cowardice, without counterpart in the histories of the most barbarous nations
monstrous ingratitude, and a resisting of God, since they had been told their lives were given to Paul
